newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends string of gains before employment data.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends string of gains before employment data.

text.p: The dollar edged lower on Thursday, ending a winning streak as traders turned cautious ahead of Friday's labour market report for September.

The dollar eked out a fresh 10-week high against the German mark before retreating in early trading. But the currency failed to climb above 112 Japanese yen -- a 32-month high set on Wednesday -- before the monthly unemployment report, which has set financial markets into a tailspin in recent months.
"It's just been a bit of profit-taking going into the employment numbers," said Tim Summerfield, senior foreign exchange trader at Bank of Boston.
"(The market) is just saying: 'We've had a nice run and done very well out of it, thank you very much,'" he added.
The dollar reached 1.5341 marks in Europe but slipped to 1.5310 marks in late trading, versus 1.5325 late Wednesday.
The dollar fetched 111.47 yen, down from a high of 111.97 yen in Tokyo and 111.87 yen late Wednesday.

Wall Street economists predict that employers added 166,000 jobs to their payrolls in September, after hiring 250,000 in August. The unemployment rate is forecast to increase slightly to 5.2 percent from 5.1 percent.

The monthly jobs report is the Federal Reserve's key barometer of economic growth and future inflation. Surprisingly high payrolls have roiled bond and currency markets on several occasions this year.

The September numbers have gained added importance since the Fed surprised the market by declining to tighten monetary policy in September, even though the economy grew more than 4 percent in the second quarter.

Traders are nervous that tight labour market conditions will produce higher inflation and spur the Fed to raise interest rates. This would depress U.S. bonds and stocks and could weaken the dollar if foreign investors decide to pare holdings of U.S. assets.
But a weak number could help the dollar by increasing investor confidence that the Fed has inflation under control.

"If we get numbers that reaffirm the Fed's decision was right, then the market might actually buy dollars, as a sense of confidence in the Fed starts to pervade the market," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan.

Meanwhile, the market still has an appetite for dollars amid consistently pro-dollar comments from several high-profile G7 officials following the gathering of finance ministers and central bankers in Washington.

In the latest comment, French President Jacques Chirac said in a French magazine interview due to appear on Saturday that the dollar is really undervalued and that coordination should be enhanced between the Fed and other big central banks to ensure its proper value.

"There is no doubt that all the officials coming out of this past weekend's G7 meetings are hitting the pavement with the same talk -- 'strong dollar,'" said Stephen Flanagan, vice president at Credit Agricole. "It is doing a lot to keep the dollar at these higher levels."
In other trading, the dollar slipped to 1.2557 Swiss francs from 1.2579 late Wednesday and rose to Canadian $1.3603 from C$1.3593. The British pound rose to $1.5655 from $1.5653.
